title: Goal and success test
plain: A goal says who the project is for and what they can do. A success test is something you can run or click that proves the goal is met, so 'done' is not a feeling.
check: Your goal is 'a recipe site my family can use'. What is one concrete test you could run to show it works, and what exactly would you see?
rubric: The goal names who it is for and what they can do
The success test is an action with a visible result, not an opinion
The learner says what result would mean 'not done yet'
try: Create a file GOAL.md in your project folder (in an editor, or ask Codex). Write two lines: 'Goal: <who> can <do what>.' and 'Success test: I run or click <exact thing> and see <exact result>.' Save it. You now have one page the AI can check its work against.
pitfall: Wrong belief: you can start building and the finished idea will become clear on the way. Correct: without a success test, neither you nor the AI can tell when to stop or whether a change broke something.

title: Smallest first version
plain: An MVP (minimum viable product) is the smallest version that does one whole job. Non-goals are features you decide not to build yet and write down, so they are not added by accident.
check: You want a todo app with accounts, sharing, reminders and a phone app. Which one thing would you build first, and what do you give up by leaving the rest for later?
rubric: The 3 steps run from the start to a useful result
Each non-goal is a real feature the learner wanted
The smallest version could be finished in one or two sessions
try: In GOAL.md (or any notes file) add a line 'Non-goals:' with three features you will not build in version 1. The next time you or Codex says 'let us also add...', read that line first. You now have a written reason to say 'later'.
pitfall: Wrong belief: a first version needs all the features, or it is not real. Correct: a small version that works from start to end shows you what users need; features added before that are guesses.

title: Folders by purpose
plain: A module is one file or folder with one clear purpose. Group files by what they are for, such as screens, data, settings and tests, so you and the AI can find things fast.
check: You add a feature that sends an email reminder. Which folder does its code go in, and what in your project's layout tells you that?
rubric: Every folder has a purpose sentence of one line
No folder is a mixed dump such as misc, stuff or utils
The learner can say where the files of a new feature would go
try: In your project folder run `ls`. It works in PowerShell, Git Bash, macOS and Linux, and prints the top-level files and folders. Next to each folder write one sentence saying what it is for. A folder you cannot describe in one sentence is a candidate to rename or split.
pitfall: Wrong belief: a folder called utils or helpers is a safe place for anything. Correct: it fills up with unrelated files and has no clear purpose; name folders after what they do for the user or the program, such as recipes, settings or payments.

title: Small files, small functions
plain: Keep each file short enough to read in one sitting and each function to one job. As a guide, look closely at files over about 300 lines and functions over about 60 lines.
check: A file has 900 lines and everything works. Why can this still be a problem for you and for Codex next month?
rubric: Finds the longest file with a command or by asking Codex
Names two different jobs in that file
Says what stays the same for the user after the split
try: Count the lines of one of your files. In Git Bash, macOS or Linux run `wc -l src/app.py` (use your own file name). In PowerShell run `(Get-Content src/app.py).Count`. You see one number; compare it with 300.
pitfall: Wrong belief: one big file is simpler because everything is in one place. Correct: a big file is hard to review and easy to break, because you and the AI must read all of it to change one thing.

title: Boring technology
plain: Boring technology means well-known tools with many users, clear docs and known ways of failing. Choose them by default, and allow at most one new tool to learn per project (an 'innovation token').
check: The AI proposes five tools for your small project, and three of them were released this year. How do you decide which to keep, and what do you check before you agree?
rubric: Each tool is marked boring or new with a reason (age, users, documentation)
At most one new tool is kept, and the learner chose it on purpose
The learner says where to read the current docs for each tool
try: Ask Codex: 'List every tool and library in this project. For each one, show the page where you checked its latest release and its documentation. Do not answer from memory.' You get a short table; any row without a source is a risk to question.
pitfall: Wrong belief: the newest tool is the best tool. Correct: the AI learned mostly from older material and may write code for a version that has changed; tools with a long record have more correct examples and known fixes.

title: Settings outside the code
plain: Configuration is anything that differs between computers, such as ports, URLs and API keys. Keep it outside the code, for example in a .env file that Git ignores, so secrets stay out of Git.
check: Sort these into code or configuration and give one reason each: an API key, the function that adds two prices, the address of your test database, the wording of a button. Which are which?
rubric: Sorts the API key and the test database address as configuration: they differ between computers, and the key is secret.
Sorts the price function and the button wording as code or content: they are the same on every computer.
Says configuration goes in a .env file that Git ignores, with a .env.example that lists the names with fake values.
try: In a scratch folder run `git init -b main`. With an editor (or Codex) create .gitignore containing the line .env, and .env containing FAKE_KEY=abc123. Then run `git check-ignore -v .env`. You see one line that starts with `.gitignore:1:.env` followed by the file name; it names the rule that hides the file.
pitfall: Wrong belief: it is fine to put a key in the code for now and move it later. Correct: once a key is committed or pasted into a chat, treat it as exposed; keep it in .env from the first line.

title: One job per part
plain: Separation of concerns means each part of a program has one job, such as showing things, applying rules or storing data. Single responsibility applies the same idea to each function and file.
check: A function reads a form, checks the price rules, saves to the database and prints a receipt. You later change how receipts look. What else could break, and why?
rubric: Lists each job in a few words (for example read input, check rules, save, show)
Proposes a split where each part has one job
Says which part changes if the screen changes and which if the rules change
try: Pick one function of 20 or more lines in your project and ask Codex: 'List every job this function does, one per line. Do not change anything.' If the list has more than one line, ask for a plan to split it. You only read the list.
pitfall: Wrong belief: splitting code into many layers is always cleaner. Correct: split along real jobs that change for different reasons; layers that hold one line each add reading cost without any benefit.

title: DRY and YAGNI
plain: DRY (don't repeat yourself): keep each piece of knowledge in one place. YAGNI (you aren't gonna need it): do not build it until needed. Rule of three: extract a shared helper on the third copy.
check: Two files each have the same 8 lines for formatting a date. The AI wants a new DateService class with settings for every date style. What do you do, and what would make you change your mind?
rubric: Counts how many places really use the code
Chooses keep, extract or delete and gives a reason
Says what happens if the rule changes in one copy but not the others
try: Ask Codex: 'Search this project for code that appears three or more times, and for classes or functions used in only one place. List both and change nothing.' Copies seen three or more times are candidates to extract; a single-use abstraction is a candidate to delete.
pitfall: Wrong belief: any repeated code must be removed at once, and extra flexibility is always good. Correct: a wrong abstraction costs more than two copies; wait until the pattern repeats and build for today's need.

title: Data model first
plain: A data model is the list of things your app stores, such as users or recipes, and the fields each one has. Decide it before designing screens, because screens and code grow from it.
check: For a recipe app, each recipe has ingredients. Would the ingredients be one long text field or their own list of items, and what could you do later with each choice?
rubric: Each thing has 3 to 8 named fields with a kind of value (text, number, date)
One field identifies each item uniquely, for example an id
At least one link between two things is shown (a recipe has many ingredients)
try: Before you build a feature, write its data in a file DATA.md: one line per thing, fields after a colon, like `Recipe: id, title, minutes, notes`. Then ask Codex to compare the file with the code and list every field the code uses that your list lacks. Nothing in the code changes.
pitfall: Wrong belief: build the screens first and the shape of the data will appear on its own. Correct: changing the shape of stored data later is one of the hardest changes, because the old data must be moved too.

title: Build or reuse
plain: Before you write a feature yourself, check whether the language, the framework or a trusted library already does it. Build your own only when nothing fits or building it is the point of your project.
check: You need to send emails from your app. Codex offers to write an email-sending module from scratch. What do you ask before accepting, and what could go wrong if you accept?
rubric: Checks the language or framework first, then libraries
Names why a library can be trusted (age, maintainers, users, documentation)
States the cost of using it and the cost of writing it yourself
try: Pick one feature from your list and ask Codex: 'Does the language, our framework or a well-known library already do this? Show me where it is documented and when it was last updated. Do not write code yet.' You get one to three options with links; open one link and find its usage page.
pitfall: Wrong belief: writing it yourself is safer because you control the code. Correct: your own code has bugs nobody has found yet; for common jobs such as dates, login or encryption, tested libraries are safer.

title: Cost of a dependency
plain: A dependency is code written by someone else that your project needs to run. Each one adds updates, bugs, licence terms and security risk, so add one only when it saves real work.
check: Codex wants to add a package that pads numbers with zeros. Which questions do you ask before you say yes, and how much code would it replace?
rubric: For each one, says what job it does in the project
Checks that it is maintained (recent release, active repository)
Says whether the lockfile is committed
try: Open the file that lists your dependencies (package.json for Node, requirements.txt for Python) and count the entries. Pick one and ask Codex: 'What does this package do for us, who maintains it, and how many lines would it take to do without it?' In a Node project, also run `ls` and look for package-lock.json, the lockfile.
pitfall: Wrong belief: a popular package is automatically safe and free to keep. Correct: each package also pulls in its own dependencies, and a package can be abandoned or taken over; fewer, well-maintained packages and a committed lockfile (package-lock.json for npm) lower the risk.

title: Contracts between parts
plain: An interface is how one part of a program asks another to do something. A contract is the agreement: what you send in, what you get back, and what happens when it fails.
check: Your web page asks the server at the address /recipes and expects a list. Someone changes the server to return an object with a 'recipes' field inside it. What breaks, and how could a written contract have prevented it?
rubric: Input fields have names and the kind of value
The output has a shape and one real example
At least one failure is described, as the caller would see it
try: Choose one function or API route your app uses. Ask Codex: 'Write its contract as plain text first: inputs, outputs, errors. Do not edit any file.' Read it, then run the program with one wrong input. If the program behaves differently from the text, one of them is wrong; that is a bug the contract just found.
pitfall: Wrong belief: if both sides are my own code, I do not need an agreement. Correct: an unwritten agreement lives only in memory; you and the AI will each guess, and changing one side silently breaks the other.

title: Where state lives
plain: State is the information your program remembers: a logged-in user, a shopping cart, saved notes. Decide for each item where it lives (memory, browser, file, database), because that decides what survives a restart.
check: A todo list is kept in a JavaScript variable in the browser. The user refreshes the page. What happens to the list, and where would you move it so that it survives?
rubric: Each item has one named home (variable, file, localStorage, database)
Correctly predicts what survives a restart
Correctly predicts what a second device sees
try: List three things your app remembers. For each one ask Codex: 'Where does this data live, and what happens to it when the program restarts?' Write your own prediction first. Then stop the program, start it again, and check which of the three are still there.
pitfall: Wrong belief: if it works on my screen, it is saved. Correct: data in a variable disappears when the program stops, and data in the browser stays on that one browser; only data saved in a database or file that the server keeps (and backs up) is shared between devices.

title: Error handling
plain: Error handling means deciding what the program does when something fails. Fail loudly with a clear message, say what to do next, set time limits on slow calls, and never hide an error.
check: Your program reads a settings file and the file is missing. What are two ways the program could react, and which one do you want and why?
rubric: Finds an empty catch or except block, or a failure that is ignored
Triggers it safely (for example with a wrong file name)
The new message says what failed and what to try
try: Search for hidden errors. In your project run `git grep -n --untracked -A2 "except"` (for JavaScript use "catch" instead; --untracked also searches files you have not added to Git yet). Look for a handler whose next line is only `pass` or empty. Each hit shows the handler and the 2 lines after it; an empty handler hides an error. You only read; ask Codex to propose a fix for one.
pitfall: Wrong belief: a program that never shows errors is working well. Correct: a hidden error makes a small bug hard to find; show or log every failure with what happened and where.

title: Logging
plain: A log is a record of what your program did, written while it runs. Log events with a level (info, warning, error) and enough context to find the cause later, but never passwords or keys.
check: A user says 'the export did not work yesterday at 3 pm'. What would you want your log to have recorded to find the cause, and what must it never contain?
rubric: Uses a level (info or error), not only print
Each line says what happened and includes a value that helps find it
No secret or personal data appears in the output
try: Run this one-line demo; it creates no files. On macOS or Linux: `python3 -c "import logging; logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO); logging.info('started'); logging.warning('disk almost full')"`. On Windows use `python` instead of `python3`. You see two lines that start with INFO:root: and WARNING:root:. Change INFO to WARNING in the command and run it again: the INFO line disappears.
pitfall: Wrong belief: print() everywhere is the same as logging. Correct: print has no level, so you cannot turn it down without editing code; a logger can be made quieter or louder by one setting, and either way you must keep secrets out of it.

title: Hard-to-undo choices
plain: Easy to undo: you can change it later in minutes, like a colour. Hard to undo: changing it means moving data or rewriting code, like the database or login. Spend care on hard ones.
check: Your app stores recipes in a JSON file and later you want a real database. What has to happen to undo the first choice, and what would have made that cheaper?
rubric: Sorts correctly: database, login method, hosting and data model are hard; names, colours and text are easy
For each hard choice, names what must be moved or rewritten
Says which hard choices need a written decision record
try: Take the list of choices Codex proposed for your project (language, database, hosting, login, folder names, colours). Write E (easy) or H (hard) next to each, and for every H one sentence: 'To undo this I would have to ...'. You get a short list; the H lines are the choices that need a decision record.
pitfall: Wrong belief: every choice matters equally, or any choice can be fixed later. Correct: most choices are cheap to change, but a few (data, login, hosting, language) are expensive; spend your thinking time on those.

title: Decision record
plain: A decision record (ADR) is a short file that says what you decided, which options you had, why you chose this one, and what would make you change your mind.
check: Six months from now, someone asks why the project uses SQLite and not PostgreSQL. Which parts of your decision record answer that, and which part tells them when to look at the choice again?
rubric: Has the question, 2 or 3 options, the decision and the reasons
Lists what you give up
Says what would change your mind
try: Create the folder docs/decisions and a file 0001-first-choice.md (in an editor, or ask Codex). Write the headings Question, Options, Decision, Why, What we give up, Change our mind when. Fill them in for one real choice, such as your database. You get one page you can read in a minute.
pitfall: Wrong belief: writing down decisions is paperwork for big companies. Correct: a one-page record saves you, and the AI in a new session, from arguing the same choice again, and shows when the choice has stopped fitting.

title: Trade-offs
plain: A trade-off means every choice gains something and costs something. Compare at least two options on the same points, such as time, money, risk and ease of change, and say what you give up.
check: Codex says 'use PostgreSQL, it is the best database'. What do you ask to find the cost of that advice, and for which kind of project would the answer be different?
rubric: Two real options, not one good and one weak
The same points are compared for both (for example setup time, cost, risk, ease of change)
States what is given up by the choice
try: Next time Codex recommends a tool, type: 'Give me two options with the cost of each, what I give up with your pick, and what would change your mind.' You see two short options with costs instead of one bare recommendation.
pitfall: Wrong belief: there is one best tool, or the first suggestion of the AI is the right one. Correct: a choice is best only for a given goal and limits; the same choice can be wrong for another project.

title: Security by default
plain: Security by default means the safe choice is the starting point: private, locked and minimal until you open something on purpose. Ask who can reach each part and what the worst case is.
check: Your app hides the delete button from normal users. Why is that not enough, and where must the rule be checked?
rubric: Names who can read and who can change each kind of data
Finds anything that is open to the whole internet
Names the worst case and one limit on the damage (backup, spending cap, test copy)
try: Ask Codex: 'List every route, port and file in this project that someone outside my computer could reach, and what each one allows. Do not change anything.' Read the list; anything you did not expect to be public is your first question.
pitfall: Wrong belief: security is a feature you add at the end, or a hidden button is protection. Correct: access rules decided at the start are cheap, and the server must check who may do what, because anyone can call a web address directly.

title: Over-built stack
plain: An over-built stack uses many services or tools for a small problem, such as microservices, queues and several frameworks. A monolith (one program, one database) is the simpler start.
check: The AI proposes separate services for users, recipes and notifications for a project you will share with ten friends. What do you ask, and what would you propose instead?
rubric: Counts the services and tools and says what each one does
Names the extra work each one adds (network calls, deployments, logs, failures)
Proposes one program with clear folders as the starting point
try: Run `git ls-files --cached --others --exclude-standard`; it lists every file that is tracked or new, but not ignored. Look for several folders that each have their own start file or a Dockerfile, or a docker-compose.yml with more than one app service. For one person, one program is usually enough. If you find several, ask Codex: 'Why is this more than one service, and what would break if we merged them?'
pitfall: Wrong belief: big companies use microservices, so good design starts with them. Correct: those companies usually split a working single program once it grew too big; every extra service adds network failures, deployments and logs to learn and fix.

title: Home-made login
plain: Custom authentication means writing your own login: storing passwords, checking them, making sessions. It is easy to get wrong. Use your framework's login or a trusted login service, which stores only password hashes.
check: A stranger copies your user table. What can they read if the passwords are stored as plain text, and what can they read if the passwords are stored as slow, salted hashes?
rubric: Finds where passwords are stored and in what form (readable text or hash)
Says whether the framework or a trusted service already provides login
Names why readable passwords and fast hashes such as MD5 are unsafe
try: Search your project for password handling: run `git grep -n --untracked -i "password"` and read the hits. Look at where a password is saved or compared. If the saved value is the same text the user typed, it is plain text. Ask Codex to switch to the framework's built-in password hashing before any real user signs up.
pitfall: Wrong belief: login is simple, a table with a name and a password is enough. Correct: passwords must be stored only as slow, salted hashes, and sessions, resets and attacks need many more details; use a tested framework login or service.

title: SQL from strings
plain: SQL injection happens when a program builds a database command by joining user text into it. Use parameterized queries instead: write the command with placeholders and pass the values separately.
check: A search box puts what the user types straight after SELECT * FROM recipes WHERE title = in the query text. What happens if the user types a single quote followed by more SQL, and what changes when you use a placeholder?
rubric: Finds the glued query
Shows an input that changes the meaning of the query (for example a quote followed by OR TRUE)
Rewrites it with a placeholder and passes the value separately
try: Search for joined SQL. Run `git grep -n --untracked -i -E "(select|insert|update|delete) .*([{+]|%s)"` and read the hits. A real problem is SQL text joined to a variable with { (an f-string), + or the % operator. The safe form puts a ? or a :name placeholder in the SQL text and passes the values separately (some database libraries write %s as the placeholder inside execute(sql, values), which is also safe). Expect some false alarms. You only read; ask Codex to fix one real hit.
pitfall: Wrong belief: cleaning the user's text by hand (removing quotes) makes joined SQL safe. Correct: hand cleaning always misses cases; placeholders keep the command and the data apart, so user text can never run as SQL.

title: Secrets in browser code
plain: Frontend code runs in the visitor's browser, so anyone can read it. A secret key placed there is public. Keep secrets on a server, and let the browser call your server instead.
check: Your React page calls a paid API with the key stored in a VITE_ variable. A visitor opens the page and presses F12. What can they get, and where should the call move to?
rubric: Lists the variables that carry the framework's public prefix
Opens the browser's page source or network tab to see what is visible
Moves any secret to server code that the browser calls
try: Run `git grep -n --untracked -E "NEXT_PUBLIC_|VITE_"`. It shows the code that reads such variables; your .env file is not searched, because Git ignores it. Other frameworks use a similar public prefix, so check yours. Every name in the result ends up readable in the browser. Check that none holds a secret key, token or password. Some keys are made to be public; the provider's docs say which. You only read; ask Codex to move any secret to server code.
pitfall: Wrong belief: a secret is safe because it sits in an environment variable. Correct: variables with the framework's public prefix (such as NEXT_PUBLIC_ or VITE_) are copied into the code sent to the browser, so only server-only variables stay private.

title: No backup
plain: A backup is a separate copy of your data you can restore after a mistake or failure. A backup you never restored may not work, so test the restore once.
check: Your app keeps everything in one SQLite file on a free hosting plan. What could remove that file, and what would you need in place to be back online within an hour?
rubric: The backup is a separate file or place, not the same folder as the live data
The restore is done once, to a different location
The restored data opens and shows the expected number of records
try: Stop the app, then copy its data file next to the original under a new name, for example `cp data.db data-backup-1.db`. This works in PowerShell, Git Bash, macOS and Linux. Open both files with your database tool, or ask Codex to count the rows in each. You should see the same number.
pitfall: Wrong belief: Git or the host already keeps my data safe. Correct: Git saves code, not the data your users create, and some hosts reset local files when the app restarts or is redeployed; keep a backup of the data in a different place.

title: Runaway paid calls
plain: A paid-API loop calls a service that charges per request over and over. A bug can repeat it all night. Cap the calls per run, add pauses, and set a spend limit with the provider.
check: A script retries a failed paid call until it works. The service is down for eight hours. What could that cost, and which three limits would you add?
rubric: Finds the loop and what stops it (a counter, a time limit, an end condition)
Finds the cost of one call and multiplies it by the worst case
Checks for a pause between retries after a failure
try: Run `git grep -n --untracked -i -E "while true|while \(true\)|setInterval|retry"` and read the hits. For each hit find what stops the loop (a counter, a time limit, an end condition) and what one pass costs. If you call a paid API, open that provider's billing page and set a spend limit before you run the loop.
pitfall: Wrong belief: the provider will stop a runaway loop for me. Correct: the provider's own monthly cap can be high; set a lower spend limit yourself, and add limits in your code too: a maximum number of calls, a pause between retries and a dry-run mode.
